“Appeasement, Ohio”

By George Saunders

Yeow, the old Ohio place. My cousin Maribeth looks about the same. Her son Kip’s a man now: big boy, around two-fifty, thick pink arms like tattooed hams.

“Eggs?” Carl says.

“No, thanks,” I say.

“I will,” Kip says.

“Scrambled,” Mick says.

“Yes, sir, still believe in chickens,” Mick says, maintaining discipline.

“Upstairs, in the attic?” Carl says. “Kip? A box of Civil War coat buttons, from your great-great-whoever. Plus his bayonet.”

“Anyone can make a button,” Mick says.

“Anyone can put a bayonet in an attic,” Kip says.

“Look how I trained him up,” Mick says.

I’m trying to connect the beaming giant that is Kip with the shy little guy I used to carry up to bed.

Carl sets down a plate of toast.

“Food for the brain trust,” he says.

“You’re being sarcastic,” says Mick.

“Ma’s a believer,” says Kip.

“Well, you kids make a strong case,” Maribeth says.

“For example,” says Kip, spinning his Dell around.

“Zero palm trees in Pennsylvania,” Carl says.

“That you know of,” Kip says.

“That anyone knows of,” Carl says.

“What’s your source?” Mick says in a faux-military voice.

“Having been there many times,” Carl says.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s interrogation of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced Theranos founder, is a compelling spectacle of manipulation, suspicion, and apparent sincerity.

By Richard Brody

Nathan Fielder may well have the best deadpan shtick since Buster Keaton. But, whereas Keaton offers stoic innocence, Fielder clinically probes other people’s misconceptions and delusions, which makes him a perfect match for Elizabeth Holmes. Holmes, the founder of Theranos, a Silicon Valley startup that purported to revolutionize blood testing, was convicted of four counts of fraud in 2022 and sentenced to more than eleven years in prison. In 2023, less than two months before the start of her sentence, she and her partner, Billy Evans, summoned Fielder to their beachfront house in Southern California and invited him to move in and film them in their domestic environment. The result is Fielder’s new documentary, “You Can See Everything,” which he co-directed with Lance Oppenheim, an experienced documentarian who also directed the recent drama “Primetime.”

One of my pet peeves with observational documentaries (including Oppenheim’s 2020 film, “Some Kind of Heaven”) is the elision of their transactional side: What do the movie’s on-camera participants expect to get from being filmed? There’s no such danger with “You Can See Everything.” Holmes states up front that she wants to correct the public narrative; she hopes that having the filmmakers in her house will enable her to be seen, as Evans puts it, with “radical transparency.” She says that she wants to present her story as “a human story”: “It starts with who I am and what my intent was and still is.” She claims to be innocent and appears bewildered by her fate. Fielder asks, with astonishment, whether she really thinks she committed no crime, and she responds, “I know I didn’t commit any crime.”

Fielder, of course, is no ordinary observational filmmaker; he has forged a TV career from drastic interventionism. His onscreen manner is based on affectlessly posing intrusive questions, and his shows involve real-life simulations akin to social-science experiments. (In his series “Nathan for You,” he forms faux businesses; in “The Rehearsal,” he directs participants in elaborate stagings of their real-life situations.) These features lend his work an air of cruelty, making people seem like specimens in the hands of a researcher bound by no scientific ethics or norms. The relationships are mainly ones of power, and he doesn’t let his subjects forget it.

In “You Can See Everything,” he doesn’t let Holmes forget it, either. He’s sarcastic to her and even embarrasses her in front of her parents, evidently assuming that, as her story is in his hands, she won’t dare push back. But Holmes’s preëxisting notoriety has its own power. Nothing Fielder discovers can top what’s already widely known, so his observations inevitably temper her public image. Fielder’s portrait of Holmes and his display of his methods turn his questioning to self-questioning, forcing him to assess, and even revise, basic assumptions about her and about life in general. The result is a movie of dazzling conundrums and vertiginous paradoxes, leading Fielder ever deeper into emotional and intellectual wilds. For all the unpleasantness of its backstory, its confrontations, its outcomes, and even, at times, Fielder’s own behavior, the film is more than fascinating and ingenious; it’s strangely, poetically, poignantly beautiful.

In November 2025, Sally Rooney submitted a witness statement to Britain’s High Court, on behalf of a co-founder of Palestine Action, Huda Ammori. The court was considering the UK government’s decision to designate Palestine Action as a terrorist group. Ammori was arguing that this constituted an authoritarian ban on protest. In support, Rooney said that her books might have to be withdrawn from sale in Britain, and that, "The disappearance of my work from bookshops would mark a truly extreme incursion by the state into the realm of artistic expression."

Almost a year later, this has come to pass. Rooney’s publisher, Faber, has taken her books off sale, with her consent, because they fear a prosecution. The Terrorism Act of 2000 makes it illegal to provide money to anyone where you have reasonable cause to suspect it might be used for the purposes of terrorism. After the 2025 ban on Palestine Action (PA), Rooney said, repeatedly, that she continues to support it, “in whatever way I can”. That constitutes a pretty firm basis for suspicion. It is also illegal to express support for a banned organisation. Rooney has made her statements of support from Ireland, where she lives. Had she made them here, she might have faced prosecution. Thousands of people in Britain have been arrested for holding signs which say, “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action”.

To be clear, the British government hasn’t banned Rooney’s books. It isn’t illegal to sell or distribute them; you can easily pick them up second-hand. Faber’s withdrawal is voluntary. Faber could, in theory, have kept the books on sale and withheld the payments, but decided that wouldn’t be fair on their author. They were under no pressure from the government to stop paying Rooney and in truth it seems unlikely that the Crown Prosecution Service would have picked this fight. But it’s a reasonable precaution for them to take.1

There is, of course, a political motivation for the withdrawal, at least on Rooney’s behalf. She wants to highlight the negative effects of the ban on PA. In this, she has been very successful. Millions of Sally Rooney readers have been shocked by this turn of events and many will blame the government. To anyone of common sense, it seems absurd that novels about the love lives of Irish millennials should be made unavailable on the basis of terrorism law. It also seems crazy that middle-class pensioners holding placards should be treated as engaging in terrorist activity. Even those who aren’t fans of Rooney’s books, or her politics, may feel sympathetic to her cause.

But what is her cause, exactly? What is actually at stake here, beyond the banning of one particular organisation?

The literary world is in no doubt: it has enthusiastically adopted Rooney’s framing of the issue, as set out in her statement to the High Court. The New Statesman has gathered an impressive list of writers and intellectuals, and Gary Lineker, to sign an open letter to the government. This is its admirably short text:

Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist. Her books must be available to the public. Their withdrawal from sale, on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation, is an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country. We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity.

The letter comes attached to an op-ed by Tanjil Rashid, editor of the New Statesman’s (superb) culture pages. It opens by invoking the name of Salman Rushdie, before going on to develop the comparison:

The last time books by a controversial author were withdrawn from retailers was during the more heated affair over The Satanic Verses. The UK government, of course, had not banned Salman Rushdie’s novel, but a climate of fear had led to its voluntary withdrawal. The government has not intentionally banned Rooney’s books either; the withdrawal of her work is equally voluntary, but based, likewise, on a climate of fear. The difference lies in how the fear has been stoked. Rushdie’s censor was terrorism – actual terrorists, who spilled real blood over his book. In Rooney’s case, it is legislation.

Now, I like (and subscribe to) the New Statesman, but I don’t like this comparison. I find it crass, even obscene, caveat and all. But we’ll get back to Rushdie. Before we do so, let’s look at the question of whether the Rooney case is really about what she and her fellow writers say it’s about.

Is it about freedom of artistic expression? Usually, when people invoke the spectre of censorship it’s because a work of art has been banned, or an artist has been punished for self-expression. But one thing all parties agree on here is that there is little politically subversive about Normal People or Intermezzo. That these books have been removed from the shelves has nothing to do with the words inside them. Nobody in government has ever sought to ban them. Their disappearance may be a secondary effect of a restriction of speech but it is not because the artist concerned, or anyone else, has had their artistic expression curbed.

Is it about the right to dissent? The New Statesman thinks so:

Rooney has shown us that the laws aren’t fit for purpose, that writers cannot always dissent from government policy with the outspokenness and commitment that is their right.

But this doesn’t seem right, either. Writers dissent vehemently and frequently from government policy on Israel every day. Insofar as Rooney has put her publisher in legal jeopardy, it is not because she has criticised the government, and in fact it is grossly misleading to imply that it is. It is because she has said, or implied, that she will give the money that she receives from the publisher to a designated terrorist organisation. That’s it. The fact that Rooney is an author is irrelevant to the legal situation. Let’s imagine she is not a writer but a businesswoman, the owner of a vegan granola brand which exports to the UK. If she happened to tell a local paper that she might use the proceeds from these sales to support Palestine Action, Waitrose would now be in the same position as Faber.

In truth this case has nothing to do with the suppression of radical art, or subversive ideas, or dissent. It’s about an illegal flow of money. For the writers and artists who signed the New Statesman letter, that might be a disappointingly prosaic way to put it, but it’s accurate. Nonetheless, we shouldn’t dismiss the free speech question entirely. Funding aside, any expression of support for Palestine Action would expose Rooney to prosecution, if she were in Britain. Those peaceful, placard-holding protestors who spent the night in a police cell can testify to that. That does seem like an objectionable curb on speech and protest, even if it’s not specifically to do with arts and letters. But I think we should be clear, once more, about what we’re objecting to.

The New Statesman’s open letter blames the withdrawal of Rooney’s books on “draconian anti-terror legislation”. Nowhere in the letter or editorial do we learn what specific law they are objecting to, or what change they would propose. We are forced to guess. Are they objecting to the proscription of terrorist organisations in general? I doubt it. Everyone seems to agree that organisations like Al-Qaeda should be banned. Are they objecting to a law which bans people from providing funds to individuals if they suspect it will end up with terrorists? I hope not - that seems pretty sensible to me.

Perhaps their objection is to the criminalisation of any expression of support for a terrorist organisation? They would be on stronger ground here. If you’re a free speech advocate, you might well argue that it should be legal to cheer on a terrorist group, even if doing so is clearly abhorrent. The signatories of that letter should ask themselves if they would be happy with the government making it legal to speak up for, or hold placards on behalf of, a neo-Nazi group like Sonnenkrieg Division, also banned under this law. Looking at the list of names, I’d be very surprised if so. I don’t think they are objecting to legislation at all. I think they are objecting to the proscription of Palestine Action under this legislation.

Now, this more tightly defined dispute might be worth taking up cudgels for. But before taking a closer look at whether PA should be proscribed, let’s mark how far we’ve travelled. We started by asking whether this is really about artistic self-expression, as Rooney and her fellow writers claim. It doesn’t seem to be. I can see why. Who wants to have that rather tedious and confined argument when we can ride the high horse of artistic expression? The Ruffian, on the other hand, is always up for a tedious argument. So let’s look at whether Palestine Action ought to be classed as a terrorist organisation and proscribed as such. A brief recap. PA was banned by the government in 2025 when Keir Starmer was Prime Minister and Yvette Cooper was Home Secretary. It came directly in the wake of the group’s attack on the RAF airbase at Brize Norton, when members of the group sprayed paint into the engines of two aircraft. There had been several prior incidents, the most serious being an attack on a subsidiary of Elbit, the Israeli arms manufacturer, at a site near Bristol, in the course of which they smashed up a lot of equipment and attacked a police officer with a sledgehammer, fracturing her spine.

The High Court overturned Cooper’s ban on the basis that she didn’t follow due process, and that the ban had a chilling effect on free speech and protest. The Court of Appeal then upheld the ban, reversing both of the High Court’s findings. Now for the Supreme Court, which considers the case on November 4. We won’t go through all the legal arguments here; let’s just say this is hardly an open and shut case, either way. Certainly, the argument for PA being classified as terrorists is not an absurd one.

The Terrorism Act’s definition of terrorism includes causing serious damage to property in order to influence the government in pursuit of a political cause. Arguably that test is too broadly defined, but PA obviously passes it. This isn’t just a matter of technical definition. The Court of Appeal cited its “Underground Manual” which advocates for the damage and destruction of targets, and for avoiding detection; the escalation of its campaign without an apparent restraint; its attacks on key national infrastructure and firms, crucial to British defence and to our assistance of Ukraine (Elbit’s British operations are major suppliers to the UK military); its covert organisation into secret cells.

So here we have a group which has carried out several attacks on property in pursuit of its political goal and which has harmed a policewoman in the process. It puts property damage at the centre of its activity. It’s committed to continuing and escalating its campaign, which involves attacks on the country’s defence infrastructure, and its structure makes it hard for the security services to stop the attacks without banning the group.

That last is a point that even the more intelligent commentaries on this affair have overlooked. It’s very hard to prevent these crimes without taking on the organisation behind them. The Atlantic’s George Packer, in a piece sharply critical of Rooney and PA, says, “[PA’s] vandals should be prosecuted under ordinary laws”. Others have said similar. The Court of Appeal’s point is that you can’t disrupt the funding and plotting of a secretive, cell-based organisation without banning it. Proscription lets counter-terrorism police go after the whole network rather than prosecuting individual offences after the damage is done.

The effects of this proscription on free speech and protest ought to be weighed in the balance, and might outweigh the security benefits of a ban. It does seem ridiculous to me that so many peaceful protesters have been arrested (although I find it hard to see this as an authoritarian curb on speech and dissent: people can protest for the Palestinian cause as loudly and vociferously as they like without fear of the law, as long as they don’t cite that particular group). And let’s take a step back, once again. Why has the legal status of this particular group become such a cause célèbre for writers and thinkers? That one is pretty easy to answer: it’s because Sally Rooney has made it so. I doubt that most of her allies know or care much about Palestine Action and its activities. They just know that they are for the Palestinians, and are keen to stand up for a novelist claiming that her free artistic expression is being curtailed. But Rooney is framing her quarrel with the British courts in this way precisely in order to make it a cause célèbre. Rooney could be supporting the Palestinians more directly via the aid charities which work there, or failing that by supporting lawful campaigns against arms exports. She might be doing that too, but she has chosen to associate herself most closely with this group. Maybe she sincerely believes that PA is disrupting the flow of arms to Israel, or maybe she is more attracted to extremity than efficacy; smashing things up is exciting.

To me, Palestine Action seems to be an exercise in symbolism, thrill-seeking and identity-fashioning (perhaps that is the artistic self-expression Rooney refers to). Regardless, this is the fight she has picked; the one that gives her a reason to go on. Her fellow writers and intellectuals might wish to join it, but I hope they have thought through why they are doing so. One notable absentee from the New Statesman list of signatories is the author that its editorial is so keen to associate with Rooney. I don’t know if Salman Rushdie was asked, although I’d be surprised if they didn’t think of him before they got to, say, Kneecap. Rushdie was targeted by an Islamist head of state for the content of his art. He lived under credible threat of murder for decades. He saw mobs of angry men burning his book. He came horribly close to losing his life when a terrorist attacked him with a knife. He has lost an eye and a good part of his best life because of what he wrote in a novel. In his recent interview with Ezra Klein, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang strenuously argued that everyone needs to calm down about AI. The interview took place in the wake of a series of alarms about safety. A bunch of autonomous agents from OpenAI had broken out of their cage and hacked into an external company. An Anthropic researcher had resigned, claiming that neither his company nor OpenAI were responsible actors. Anthropic’s CEO had called for a co-ordinated slowdown in development.

Huang insisted to Klein that this was all a fuss about not very much. It’s simple, he said. An AI model is like any other product: if it’s not safe to release, you don’t release it, and if AI companies haven’t realised that already they will be forced to once they get hit by liability law suits. This should be no more difficult to fix than an unsafe car design. LLMs are software, and if a software product has a flaw - such as that it’s liable to wreak havoc on the world - then you fix the flaw. This is an engineering problem, not some existential mystery or intractable coordination challenge. The doomsters are spreading panic unnecessarily, and governments need to get out of the way.

Now, I am not an AI doomer. Partly through reading and cogitation, and partly through inchoate optimism, I tend to think we’ll work this one out. Even so, I found Huang’s arguments shockingly thin. The whole reason people are so scared by and excited about this technology - the whole reason Nvidia is the most valuable company in the world - is that it isn’t just software as we know it, but a new form which is by definition harder to control, since it’s probabilistic rather than deterministic, and behaves according to internal calculations which are opaque to its creators.

A second, gaping hole in Huang’s argument was his assumption that safety is a simple internal choice for individual AI labs, rather than a cost that will always get cut under intense competitive pressure, without binding regulation. This is before we get into some of Huang’s other opinions, such as that we needn’t worry about the erosion of human skills, since he can’t even remember his own address.

Ezra Klein seemed unconvinced by Huang too but had trouble standing up to the water-cannon force with which his interlocutor speaks. Huang’s speed of delivery, his unshakeable conviction, and the sense of latent anger just beneath his politeness, make him a difficult interviewee to grapple with. Dwarkesh Patel did a little better earlier in the year, on a different topic: whether or not Nvidia should be allowed to sell chips to China. Once again Huang’s arguments were perfectly aligned with his commercial incentives (why yes, of course we should!) and flimsy as paper.

Patel pushed Huang enough to rile him. My favourite moment came after Patel suggested that the Chinese, after taking advantage of American chips, would then push Nvidia and others out of the market. Huang exclaimed: “You’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser! That loser attitude, that loser premise makes no sense to me!”1

That is not an argument at all, is it? It’s a furious assertion of will which overrides all intelligent inquiry, logic and nuance. And it says a lot about why Huang has founded a multi-trillion dollar company when almost everyone else on the planet has not.

Share

The nagging question I always have when listening to Huang say things like this is, “Does he know he’s being stupid?” I use the adjective advisedly. I don’t think he’s stupid at all, for obvious reasons, and in his domain at least, he’s orders of magnitude cleverer than me. But that’s the point. How can someone so demonstrably clever make such obviously flawed arguments?

One answer to this is a Marxist-Machiavellian one: of course Huang knows he’s talking rubbish. He is saying this stuff to advance his material interests and those of his shareholders. While we can’t rule that out, that is not the impression I get. Huang really seems to believe what he says. In fact, if he didn’t, he might choose to make his false arguments subtler and more persuasive. My model of Huang is that he is delusional, but in just the right ways and to just the right extent for the job he does.

In 1989, the psychologist Roy Baumeister coined the term “optimal margin of illusion”. Baumeister’s theory was that a small measure of self-deception helps people to be happy. People who assess themselves and their prospects with ruthless accuracy are more vulnerable to depression and paralysis. This is “depressive realism”. Happy people view reality through a slightly fuzzy filter. A modest distortion is adaptive, but if our confidence gets too high we start making disastrous decisions.

The empirical evidence for Baumeister’s hypothesis is mixed. There is certainly evidence that “self-enhancement” - unrealistically positive views about yourself - is associated with greater happiness. There is less evidence for “depressive realism”. Depressed people often have negative illusions about themselves; this review found that, on average, depressed people make slightly less accurate judgements. Nobody has established where the optimal margin of illusion lies, or if there is one.

But I find Baumeister’s idea very useful. It certainly seems to apply to entrepreneurs. Huang seems to have an optimal margin of illusion about himself and his business. If he was totally delusional he would be a failed entrepreneur, constantly telling himself that the next business would be the unicorn. But if he was more realistic than he is, he would probably be running a decently-sized chipmaking company for computer games instead of a world-conquering behemoth.

In 2006, Huang made Nvidia spend hundreds of millions adding software to graphics chips so that they could do much more complicated maths, out of a vague but firmly held belief that there would be a big market in computing for science and engineering. Nvidia’s shareholders thought it was bonkers - people bought Nvidia chips to play video games, not to do science. But Huang forced the investment through, no doubt projecting the same mesmeric confidence in his judgement that he does in interviews.

Then came the AI revolution. The new chips turned out to be perfect for the complex calculations needed for deep learning and then LLMs, and Nvidia was on its way to becoming the lynchpin of the biggest financial boom in 200 years. Huang didn’t know that was going to happen. He just knew he wasn’t a loser. He made an irrational bet on an unrealistic intuition, and it paid off.

If this sounds like I’m trying to diminish his achievement, I’m not. In a sense, this is what successful entrepreneurship is. It’s living inside the optimal margin of illusion for the marketplace. In The Theory of Moral Sentiments Adam Smith blended economic theory with psychology to tell the story of “the poor man’s son” seduced by a grand, self-deceiving illusion: that great wealth will bring great happiness (Smith was somewhat suspicious of wealth as a personal ambition, even though he deemed it a social good).

The man toils away for years, flattering people he despises and serving people he hates. In old age, he finally realises that wealth - mere “trinkets” - hasn’t made him happy at all. Smith wasn’t arguing that the man’s ambition was folly. His point was that illusions are a source of energy and action. Social progress, he argued, depends upon self-deception, which “rouses and keeps in continual motion the industry of mankind.”

Self-deception also generates more risk-taking. Huang “got lucky” with the sudden emergence of LLMs as a massive source of demand for his fancy chips. But his margin of illusion put him in the right place at the right time to take advantage of it.

Of course, this means that entrepreneurs like Huang are rather unreliable witnesses to reality. Huang is single-minded in the most extreme sense: his whole cognitive function is bent towards the goal of advancing his business. That doesn’t mean we should dismiss everything he says. The rigours of the market mean he has to stay at least somewhat close to reality. Much closer, in a way, than most of us. Every day he processes a lot of information about his business, about technology and finance and politics (which apparently means he’s got no room left over for his home address), and responds in mostly sensible ways.

But where reality comes into sharp conflict with his business vision, it’s no contest. He constructs an illusory narrative in which LLMs are just software, safety is a mere engineering problem, and China will always find his American chips preferable to domestically made ones. That makes him say stupid things but without the stupidity he might not act in a way that grows his business, and that would be almost literally unthinkable.

I quite like Huang. When I reviewed his biography last year I suggested that its title, The Thinking Machine, was less than apt. Compared to his somewhat bloodless peers like Zuckerberg or Amodei, he is vividly human, a real poor man’s son with a furnace inside him and the charisma of a populist politician. But in this one sense he does resemble an LLM: he hallucinates. And as with LLMs, his hallucinations are a structural feature of his effectiveness rather than a bug.

Wie luistert, krijgt soms iets te horen wat iemand lang voor zichzelf heeft gehouden. Dat vraagt om een grote terughoudendheid in het oordeel. Ook in het milde oordeel, hoe vreemd dat ook klinkt. Zo voelt het nu voor mij.

Ik herken bij mezelf de neiging om iemand die zich schaamt gerust te willen stellen. Om te laten weten dat er ook anders naar zijn of haar leven gekeken kan worden. Daar kan veel menselijkheid in schuilgaan. Maar wat gebeurt er wanneer mijn verlangen om iemand gerust te stellen sneller is dan mijn bereidheid om te begrijpen waar die schaamte vandaan komt?

Die vraag hoort voor mij bij de ethiek van het luisteren.

De ander

Roger Burggraeve wees me op een recent boek van Aïda N’Diaye, La honte. Quand le regard de l’autre nous façonne, De schaamte. Wanneer de blik van de ander ons vormt.(12). In de beschrijving van het boek staat een zin: « La honte est une émotion singulière. Elle est partout – dans nos corps, nos silences, nos imaginaires, nos relations. » Schaamte zit ergens in ons lichaam, in onze stiltes, in wat we ons voorstellen, in hoe we met elkaar leven. N’Diaye laat zien hoe het ontstaat onder de blik van anderen, en hoe het zich van daaruit kan verplaatsen: van wie iets heeft aangedaan naar wie iets is aangedaan. Haar voorstel is om te leren leven met schaamte, met « cette marque qui nous définit », datgene dat ons kenmerkt. Ook dat vraagt iets van wie luistert.

Luisteren vraagt dat ik kan verdragen dat de ander iets ervaart wat ik zelf anders zou beoordelen. Dat ik ruimte laat voor een wereld die mij vreemd is. Zeker wanneer schaamte voortkomt uit overtuigingen die ik zelf niet deel.

Bij die vrouw speelde dat verschil tussen ons ongetwijfeld een rol. Ik keek anders naar de liefde waarover ze vertelde. Haar angst voor de hel stond ver van mij af. Wat had ik van haar kunnen leren als ik langer bij die angst was gebleven?

Het is verleidelijk om achteraf te bedenken welke vraag ik had moeten stellen. Ik had haar kunnen vragen wie haar had geleerd dat het verkeerd was om van meer dan één mens te houden. Of wat ze zelf van die liefde vond, los van de straf waarvoor ze bang was.

Maar ook dat zijn mijn vragen, voortgekomen uit mijn eigen denken. Wat zij op dat moment nodig had, is een andere vraag.

Ze heeft mij iets toevertrouwd wat voor haar heel moeilijk was want ze het nog nooit aan niemand verteld. Ze vond de woorden om over die andere man te vertellen, terwijl ze wist dat haar leven bijna voorbij was. En kort daarna is ze overleden.

Of ze uiteindelijk met meer rust heeft kunnen sterven, zal ik nooit weten.

Wat ik al die jaren nooit ben vergeten, is haar schaamte over een liefde die kennelijk nooit helemaal uit haar leven was verdwenen. Die schaamte zorgde voor een grote angst voor de hel.’. Ik denk aan de plaats die die man in haar hart had behouden, naast de liefde voor haar echtgenoot. En ik vraag me af hoeveel van ons een oordeel met zich meedragen dat ooit van buiten kwam en inmiddels zo eigen is geworden dat we er nauwelijks nog afstand van kunnen nemen.

Deze week heeft die vrouw mij, jaren na haar dood, opnieuw aan het denken gezet. Ook over mijn eigen luisteren. Wat ik nu graag aan haar had willen vragen, is waar of van wie ze had geleerd zich voor dat grote hart te schamen.

Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts.

Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence, I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence, I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.”

“This is the worst AI you will ever use”

I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence, and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI.

But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone.

We are living in an exponential

The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. The benchmark measured the amount of human work that an AI can do with at least a 50% chance of success from a single prompt. Gains on this benchmark have been startlingly regular. From the release of GPT-4 to the end of the METR measure, the amount of work AI could do doubled eight times. In 2024, an AI could do a four minute task. At the moment I turned in my draft of Co-Existence in April of 2026, an AI could do 17 hours of human work.

And then the benchmark ran out.

METR said they could no longer accurately measure the amount of work an AI could do using their current methods. Other studies suggest that number might be 17 weeks of work, or more.

And, even as ability has increased, prices have dropped. My old favorite AI benchmark, the Google Proof Question and Answer Exam, which gives the AI problems that regularly stump graduate students, used to cost 30 cents in AI usage to get a single correct answer. Now, it costs four hundredths of a cent to get the same result.

How humans work with AI is changing

Despite all the progress, the frontier of AI ability is still jagged, just as it was 30 months ago. Some areas have stayed stubbornly weak (AI is still quite a bad long-form writer), while others, like solving math problems, went from terrible to superhuman in the same period. And, as I discuss in the book, even where AI is excellent, small gaps create large needs for humans, at least for now.

But AI’s gains have been so large that how we work with it has to change. In Co-Intelligence, I wrote about centaur work (divided between AI and humans) and cyborg work (blended between AI and humans). Both keep you in the loop… but you can only be in so many loops at once. Now that we have real agents, I added a third way to work with AI: the conjurer. Conjurers summon agents when needed, assign them work, and evaluates what comes back. The charts in this post were made that way: I summoned agents, gave some general guidance, and I said “make it better” a lot. It is the most powerful way to use AI, and it carries new risks as we lose control over what, exactly, the AI is doing to get us those results.

The Otter Test has fallen

Regular readers will know that I have been testing AI image generation and movie tools with the prompt “Otter on an Airplane Using Wifi” for the past few years. This is what the best image generator, Midjourney, produced 30 months ago.

So today I asked Opus 5.5 the following (typos and all, prompting has become much less important as AIs get better): “I have a post showing the what happened over the past 30 months of AI in honor of my new book (published 30 months after the origina). i want you to make the ultimate otter on an airplane using wifi video. just something fantastic, i know you are creative, give it a go.” Using my subscriptions to various online services from Google and ElevenLabs, it produced the following. (Turn the sound on)

The video has a few flaws. But the AI figured out how to make it, from the script to the images to the concept to the music to the technical aspects of creating all of this, without any help from me. That is what has changed.

This is the least we will ever talk about AI

As a result of all of these gains, AI is only becoming a bigger issue in the world. This timeline of achievements and controversies since Co-Intelligence came out gives you some idea of how much is happening (I am leaving out hundreds of important events, but, even with the power of AI, we are all having trouble keeping up).

Of course, the speed of AI advancement is a problem for an author like me, which is why my new book does not try to keep up with the news or the latest model releases. Rather, it focuses on trends like the ones in this post: AI is improving exponentially but unevenly, and the way we use it is shifting from chatbots to agents that do real work. The book is about what that means for the humans who have to co-exist with these systems: where we still have an advantage (I argue it comes down to deep knowledge, wide knowledge, taste, and agency), when to hand work to AI, and when to avoid it entirely. If you understand the trends, the present (and near future) becomes much less surprising.

<![CDATA[Kleine Overwinningen]]>https://sandervanopzeeland.substack.comhttps://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!idNy!,w_256,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89af2cf8-13bc-46d1-9768-ca7bcb761018_183x183.pngKleine Overwinningenhttps://sandervanopzeeland.substack.comSubstackMon, 26 Oct 2026 08:02:12 GMT<![CDATA[Grappige kinderen]]>https://sandervanopzeeland.substack.com/p/grappige-kinderenhttps://sandervanopzeeland.substack.com/p/grappige-kinderenSun, 25 Oct 2026 08:02:01 GMT‘Kinderen zeggen de grappigste dingen!’

Ik heb die uitspraak vaak voorbij horen komen en daarom dacht ik: laat ik de proef eens op de som nemen.

Even voorstellen: ik ben Ruben de Beer, eigenaar van comedyclub ‘De Lachparade’ in Amsterdam Oud-West. We zijn in onze club niet bang om risico’s te nemen en een betaald optreden van een grappig kind leek me een leuk en vernieuwend idee.

Na een weekje netwerken en rondbellen had ik een goede kandidaat voor mijn experiment gevonden: Timmy de Vries. Timmy voldeed aan al mijn voorwaarden: zeven jaar oud, guitige uitstraling en bovendien de plechtige verzekering van zijn ouders dat hij in gezelschap geregeld ‘de meest hilarische dingen’ zei.

Nadat Timmy had toegezegd, zette ik onmiddellijk mijn marketingafdeling (Gerrie en rooie Tina) aan het werk. Ze regelden een interview met Timmy in de buurtkrant en hingen posters door de hele stad: een close-up van Timmy’s lachende gezichtje, met daaronder in grote gouden letters de tekst:

Timmy de Vries, het nieuwe gezicht van de Nederlandse comedy.

Ik had Timmy geboekt in onze grote zaal, waar 150 mensen in passen. Binnen een dag was het uitverkocht, en dat verbaasde me niks. Comedyliefhebbers zijn altijd op zoek naar het nieuwste jonge talent, en nieuwer en jonger dan Timmy was nog nooit vertoond.

Op de zaterdagavond van het optreden heette ik Timmy en zijn moeder rond een uur of zeven welkom in onze foyer. Tijdens een drankje in onze huisbar stak ik mijn jonge ontdekking een hart onder de riem. Ik vertelde Timmy dat hij tijdens het optreden vooral veel ‘plezier’ moest hebben en dat een gemiddeld solo-optreden bij ons een uur duurde, maar dat ik een steengoede vijftig minuten ook zou accepteren. Timmy knikte braaf. Hij maakte een wat nerveuze indruk, maar dat begreep ik best gezien de omstandigheden.

Om kwart over acht liep Timmy – zijn blonde haartjes strak naar achter gekamd en gekleed in een smoking die zijn moeder voor hem had gekocht – het podium op.
Het openingsapplaus was gul en de eerste minuut van het optreden was een doorslaand succes. Timmy begon met niks meer dan zijn naam en leeftijd.

‘Ik ben Timmy! Zeven jaar oud, maar al bijna acht!’

Die opmerking scoorde gelijk een lach, en het vervolg (‘Goh, wat is deze microfoon groot!’) nog een hardere.

Mooi! Het publiek had er duidelijk zin in en de gunfactor was hoog.

Ik was op de eerste rij gaan zitten, naast Timmy’s moeder, die me op dit punt van het optreden een enthousiaste stomp tegen mijn schouder gaf.

Timmy’s eerste grap viel eveneens goed.

‘Mijn moeder zegt dat ik te veel op mijn mobiel zit. Dus vandaag ben ik op een stoel gaan zitten!’

Aardig woordgrapje. Sterke reactie vanuit de zaal.

Zijn tweede grap werkte iets minder, maar nog steeds zeer behoorlijk.

‘Mijn papa zegt dat hij thuis de baas is, maar hij zet wel altijd het vuilnis buiten als mama het vraagt. Dat is raar, toch?’

Dit vond ik op zich een aardige observatie, maar ook wat voor de hand liggend, met bovendien een onnodige toevoeging aan het einde.

Rond grap drie begon het mis te gaan.

‘Mijn juf zegt dat ik goed moet opletten in de klas, omdat ik anders geen baan krijg.
Nou, liever geen baan dan later lerares worden.’

Nu werd het onduidelijk. En zelfs een beetje onsympathiek.
De lach na de punchline was zachter en stierf bijna onmiddellijk weg, waarna alleen nog een paar over de zaal verspreide kuchjes te horen waren.
Ik keek op mijn horloge.

We waren twee minuten bezig.

Ik begon langzaam door te krijgen op welke comedystijl Timmy mikte.
Droge oneliners.
Maar die stijl is een stuk moeilijker dan het lijkt.
Ik vermoed dat hij zelf ook onraad rook, want na zijn derde grap bleef Timmy weifelend en zwijgend aan de voorkant van het podium staan, hinkelend van het ene been op het andere.

Daarna nam hij zijn desastreuze besluit.

‘Mag ik u wat vragen?’ begon hij tegen een dikke man op rij twee.
‘Oh God, nee’, mompelde ik zachtjes.
Improvisatie.
Bij uitstek een comedyvorm waar beginners zich nooit aan moeten wagen.

‘Waar komt u vandaan?’ vroeg Timmy.
‘Uit Amsterdam!’ riep de dikke man.
‘Oh,’ zei Timmy, en dan – na een veel te lange stilte – ‘Ik ook!’
Ik sloeg de handen voor mijn gezicht.
Nu stootte de moeder van Timmy me aan.
‘Het gaat wel goed, toch?’ fluisterde ze zenuwachtig.
Ik deed net of ik haar niet gehoord had.

Timmy keek nu een paar seconden naar de grond.
‘Ik heb het warm’ stotterde hij uiteindelijk.

Kille stilte vanuit de zaal.

Dit had ik zien aankomen. Timmy had vijf minuten lang kunnen teren op zijn uiterlijk en leeftijd, maar nu was zijn krediet verbruikt.
Naast mij stond Timmy’s moeder op. ‘Doe dat verhaal over je konijn!’ schreeuwde ze – verstaanbaar voor het hele publiek – richting podium.
‘Ik weet het niet meer!’ schreeuwde Timmy. Er stonden nu tranen in zijn ogen en tot mijn afschuw zag ik dat er zich rond het kruis van zijn broek een donkere vlek begon af te tekenen.

Onacceptabel!

(Voor de duidelijkheid: incontinentie kan tijdens een optreden best een leuke zijstap zijn, maar wanneer context en opbouw ontbreken, maakt het een amateuristische en ronduit onsmakelijke indruk).

Na tien minuten, om precies vijf voor half negen, rende Timmy – nadat hij het publiek voor ‘stommeriken’ had uitgemaakt – huilend de coulissen in. Geholpen door mijn twintig jaar comedy-ervaring wist ik onmiddellijk wat me te doen stond.
Ik schoot uit mijn stoel, klom in een flits het podium op en pakte de microfoon. Nadat ik applaus voor Timmy had gevraagd, vertelde ik wat eigen grappen en verhalen om de avond nog een beetje te redden.
Maar het was te laat.
Al mijn materiaal was al eerder – en met succes – getest, maar vanavond sloeg niks meer aan. Zelfs mijn meest succesvolle stuk (over wat ik zou doen als ik een lul van een halve meter had) werd ontvangen met niks meer dan ingehouden gegrinnik. Het was duidelijk: kleine Timmy’s optreden had alle lach en goodwill uit de zaal gezogen.

Een kwartier later bood ik mijn excuses aan en beloofde het publiek zijn geld terug.

Na afloop sprak ik Timmy in de kleedkamer serieus toe.
Ik bleef rustig en beleefd, maar maakte hem wel glashelder duidelijk dat hij nog een heel, heel lange weg te gaan heeft als comedian.

Aan het einde van de avond, toen het meeste publiek al naar huis was en ik in onze huisbar mijn irritatie stond weg te drinken, sprak Timmy’s moeder me aan. Ze zei dat het haar speet, maar vroeg ook of Timmy, over een jaar of tien, nog eens zou mogen terugkomen.
‘Wanneer hij wat meer levens- en comedy-ervaring heeft opgebouwd.’

‘Natuurlijk,’ zei ik.
Maar ik verwacht er eerlijk gezegd weinig van.

Gevoel voor comedy is niet aan te leren.
Dat heb je of dat heb je niet.

Te veel volk op elkaar gepakt; schreeuwende kinderen, ladderzatte mensen die tegen me aan botsten en een misselijkmakende frituurlucht die als een kleffe deken boven de stad hing.
Ik stond op het punt om terug naar huis te vluchten toen ik het kleine grasveld in mijn buurtparkje passeerde.
Hier was het rustiger.
Aan de rand van het veldje zat een klein meisje met blonde paardenstaartjes in kleermakerszit op het gras. Toen ze oogcontact maakte, zwaaide ze vrolijk naar me. Daarna wees ze naar de tekst op haar witte T-shirt.

Persoonlijke waarheid: een euro.

Hoe oud zou ze zijn? Acht? Zes?
Waarom zat dit kind hier helemaal alleen?
Toen ik haar een euro had gegeven, beantwoordde ze mijn ongestelde vraag.
‘Ik ben op een rustig plekje gaan zitten, anders kunnen de klanten me niet verstaan!’
Ze praatte met een schattig hoog, zangerig stemmetje, zoals je verwacht bij kleine meisjes met blonde paardenstaartjes, en voor het eerst vandaag voelde ik me enigszins op mijn gemak.
‘Kom maar op met je waarheid,’ zei ik, zo vriendelijk mogelijk, de aandrang onderdrukkend om me voorover te buigen en het meisje vaderlijk (maar waarschijnlijk ongewenst) over de bol te aaien.

‘Wilt u beginnen met een zachte, doorsnee of harde waarheid?’ vroeg ze.
‘Toe maar, drie waarheden! Kost me dat extra geld?’
‘Nee, dat is inbegrepen.’
‘Begin dan maar met de zachte waarheid.’
Het meisje knikte, alsof ze dit had verwacht.
‘U heeft zich slecht geschoren. U neemt er de tijd niet voor; dat komt voort uit onrust.’
Ik voelde snel aan mijn kin.
‘Dat heb je goed gezien, mevrouwtje.’
Het compliment werd koeltjes in ontvangst genomen.
‘Doorsnee waarheid?’ vroeg het meisje.
‘Natuurlijk. Ik ben benieuwd.’
Ze keek omhoog en bestudeerde mijn gezicht zeker vijf seconden lang voor ze weer sprak.
‘U slaapt al maanden slecht,’ zei ze. ‘U voelt zich eenzaam, denkt dat niemand u begrijpt, en dat de hele wereld het op u gemunt heeft.’
Ik schoot in de lach.
‘Dat is... dat is wel heel serieus ineens, mevrouwtje.’
Het meisje knikte. ‘Dit is een serieus vak,’ piepte ze.
Ik wilde luchtig reageren, zeggen dat het allemaal wel meeviel, maar in plaats daarvan zweeg ik. Ik kon het niet ontkennen: ik sliep slecht de laatste maanden en dat de wereld het op me gemunt had, was meer dan zomaar een gedachte; het was honderd procent de waarheid. Geen idee waarom, maar alles in mijn leven was tot mislukken gedoemd. Zo was het altijd geweest en zou het altijd zijn.

Nu plaatste het meisje haar handen op het gras en keek me strak aan.
‘Harde waarheid?’
Voor ik iets kon zeggen, stak ze haar wijsvingertje onheilspellend in de lucht.
‘Ik zou het niet doen,’ fluisterde ze op een toon waarop alle jeugdigheid uit was verdwenen. ‘De harde waarheid is vaak erg naar, en de meeste klanten kunnen daar niet goed tegen.’
Dat klonk als een uitdaging.
‘Kom maar op, mevrouwtje,’ riep ik.
‘U mag me niet onderbreken tijdens mijn verhaal. Oké?’
Ik beloofde het.

Het meisje boog zich voorover, pakte mijn rechterhand, kneep erin en liet hem daarna los, begeleid door een korte zucht.
Nu knikte ze, alsof een diepe waarheid zich aan haar had geopenbaard.
‘U saboteert zichzelf,’ begon ze. ‘Daardoor wordt u boos en omdat u steeds boos bent, stoot u mensen af.’
‘Nou, ik weet niet of...’
‘Niet onderbreken!’
‘Sorry.’
‘U vindt dat de wereld u iets moet geven. Centjes, geluk, en vooral liefde. Maar liefde krijgt u niet vanzelf, meneer. Mensen die de hele tijd op zoek zijn naar liefde, alsof het een soort van product is, die gaan het nooit vinden. Er is maar één oplossing...’
‘Wat?’ schreeuwde ik.
‘U moet zelf de liefde zijn,’ zei het meisje.

Nu stond ze op, diep zuchtend, alsof de monoloog haar enorm veel energie had gekost.
‘Was dat het?’ vroeg ik.
‘Dat was het!’ zei het meisje, handen in de zij, ineens helemaal opgeklaard.
Ik schudde mijn hoofd.
‘Ik moet zelf... liefde zijn? Wat bedoel je daarmee?’
Het meisje haalde zwijgend haar schouders op.
Het was duidelijk: onze sessie was officieel voorbij.

Op weg naar huis probeerde ik mezelf moed in te praten.

Ze riep maar wat.
Vage onzin die ze in een boek heeft gelezen.
Kindergeleuter.

Maar met elke stap werden mijn twijfels groter en luidruchtiger.

Saboteerde ik mezelf?
Was alles dat misging in het leven mijn eigen schuld?
En ‘Je moet zelf liefde zijn’, wat betekende dat in hemelsnaam?

Thuis, zittend op de bank in de woonkamer, probeerde ik de situatie objectief te analyseren. Niks aan de hand. De onrust die ik voelde kwam voort uit slaapgebrek, dat was alles. Het was nu zaak om rustig te blijven en vooral geen overhaaste, irrationele beslissingen te nemen.

Een minuut later rende ik op een drafje terug naar het park.

Ik had nog drie euro in mijn zak; meer dan geld genoeg om het meisje te dwingen me nadere uitleg te geven.
Honderd meter van het grasveldje verwijderd zag ik dat de situatie was veranderd. Er stond nu een klein limonadestandje op de plek waar het meisje had gezeten. Even dacht ik angstig dat mijn kans was verkeken.
Maar nee, daar stond ze, achter een klein houten tafeltje, druk bezig bekertjes uit te delen aan dorstige klanten. De rij was zo lang dat ik pas na een minuut of vijf aan de beurt was.
‘Vertel je geen waarheden meer?’ vroeg ik, geforceerd glimlachend terwijl ik wat zweet van mijn voorhoofd veegde.
‘Nee, dat bracht niks op,’ zei het meisje. ‘Frisdrank verkoopt een stuk beter!’
Nu begonnen er mensen achter me te dringen.
‘Sorry, u houdt de rij op,’ zei het meisje. Ze klonk vriendelijk, maar haar gezichtsuitdrukking was die van een geharde zakenvrouw.
In paniek schreeuwde ik de eerste vraag die me te binnen schoot.

‘Het komt wel goed, toch? Uiteindelijk?’

Eerst dacht ik dat het meisje me niet had gehoord. Pas toen ik uit de rij was gestapt en de volgende klant mijn plaats had ingenomen, kwam het antwoord. Zonder me aan te kijken, terwijl ze vanuit een grote kan voorzichtig een plastic bekertje vol met rode limonade schonk, riep ze:
‘Tuurlijk joh. Waarom niet?’

Het klinkt misschien raar, maar dat gaf me toch wel een goed gevoel.
